Chapter 209: 0206 Definitely More Than 100 Million US Dollars

Was a valuation of 100 million US dollars outrageous?

Bokee.com, whose market share was being wildly eroded by Sina Blog and had failed in its transition to a portal site, could still be valued at 50 million US dollars in 2006 even after its valuation was halved!

Zhanzuo.com, which was being completely suppressed by Chen Guiliang's Xiaonei, was also currently having Sequoia Capital pull some strings, trying to bring SIG in for a Series B financing round. The preliminary valuation was 40 million US dollars...

And ByteDance's valuation was definitely not as simple as just 100 million US dollars.

Because Tudou alone would be valued at twenty to thirty million US dollars, and ByteDance was a shareholder of Tudou.

In the just-begun year of 2006, international capital investment in China's internet industry was about to enter a state of frenzy and blindness!

While Chen Guiliang was holding the annual meeting for his company, the China Internet Network Information Center released an authoritative statistical report: as of the end of 2005, China had 45.9 million internet-connected computers, and the total number of Chinese netizens was approximately 111 million.

The global number of netizens was only 970 million.

Over in Shanghai, Wang Wei attended a class reunion before the Spring Festival.

Yes, he met an old classmate and started dating her.

He recalled the supplementary clause in Tudou's financing agreement, which required signing some sort of prenuptial agreement. He felt that something was off.

Far away in Hangzhou, Tao Chenggang had absolutely no interest in dating.

With the Spring Festival approaching, two new games were launched in the Chinese online gaming market!

One was Object Software's *Aoshi OL*. This was the online version of *Aoshi Sanguo*, which had accumulated a large number of fans from its early single-player game days.

Its single-player version was the first Chinese game to participate in the E3 Expo in the United States and was translated into 16 languages for global release.

Including Tao Chenggang, Chinese game companies were very wary of *Aoshi OL*. One by one, they treated it as a major enemy, secretly planning various events to intercept the upcoming launch of *Aoshi OL*.

The other new game was Shanda's licensed *Dungeons & Dragons Online*!

This game had already exploded in the European and American markets, expanding wildly under the pressure of *World of Warcraft*.

There was actually a third new game, Tencent's *QQ Sonic*, but everyone had always ignored Tencent's games, not considering them enemies at all.

"Gang-ge, after Hangzhou, Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, our game has already been rolled out to internet cafes in Pengcheng, Jinling, Rongcheng, Jiangcheng, and Mindu!"

"The next step is Shancheng, Chang'an, Luzhou, Shangdu, Shimen..."

Yang Yuhui was reporting to Tao Chenggang.

He used to run a gold farming studio and knew a bit about computer technology, but wasn't an expert. Now he was mainly responsible for internet cafe promotions and had already built a team of a hundred people, with each group of 20 heading to major cities.

They promoted the game in one internet cafe after another, attracting them to cooperate by offering profits from consigned point cards.

Tao Chenggang said over the phone: "You've all worked hard. Tell the brothers to grit their teeth and push through the New Year period. In February, I'll give them triple pay, and their performance bonuses will be doubled!"

"Haha, when they hear the news, they'll definitely work twice as hard," Yang Yuhui laughed. "After the Spring Festival, I plan to recruit another 40 people."

Tao Chenggang said: "Recruit another 80. Fill the internet cafes in the municipalities and provincial capitals as soon as possible, and then launch a full-scale advance into the second, third, and fourth-tier cities."

*Power and Hegemony* had already transitioned from a non-wipe beta to an open beta in mid-January, and its current peak concurrent user count had surpassed 250,000.

Of course, this was the best data from a holiday event.

Normally, the peak concurrent user count was about 120,000, occasionally reaching 150,000 on weekend nights.

Don't think that's too few.

In the current Chinese online gaming market, there were only about 10 games in total that could maintain these numbers. And this was including casual games like *Audition Online*.

For a direct comparison during the same period, *Perfect World*'s peak concurrent user count during events was only 150,000.

*QQ Fantasy*, in order to retain and attract new players, had been running crazy events and promotions continuously, and had now pulled its concurrent user count back up to over 400,000.

This attracted a large number of studios, leading to economic inflation in the *QQ Fantasy* game. At the same time, more and more players were reaching the max level, not knowing what to do, with only highly repetitive dungeons and quests available.

It was estimated that after the Spring Festival events ended, *QQ Fantasy*'s online user count would drop again.

"Old Tao, we've confirmed over 6,000 accounts using offline bots. And almost all the studios are using them." Luo Xiaoping, a founding shareholder and the head of technology, rushed over.

Tao Chenggang said: "Ban all of them. And post these accounts on the official website."

Luo Xiaoping said: "Some paying users are also using offline bots. Two of them have cumulatively recharged over 50,000 yuan. A few others have recharged over 10,000 yuan."

"Ban them all permanently, and make an in-game announcement explaining the situation," Tao Chenggang said.

Luo Xiaoping hesitated for a few seconds, then nodded: "Okay!"

In those years, every game was flooded with cheats.

*Power and Hegemony* had only been online for three and a half months, and they had even managed to create offline bots.

*World of Warcraft* was also plagued with cheats, and The9 was about to launch "Operation Netwind," banning 120,000 accounts within a month.

On the very day *Power and Hegemony* issued the bans, a large number of angry posts appeared on its 17173 forum and Tieba.

"F*ck you, Tao Chenggang, I've spent over 60,000 in the last few months. You f*cking banned me without even a heads-up! I even supported you and promoted you everywhere... F*ck..."

"Hahaha, good riddance. Everyone hates a cheater."

"No heads-up? The game announcements have been telling people not to use cheats every day, warning you that severe cases would result in a ban."

"Gang-ge is awesome, even banning someone who spent over 60,000. I'm a die-hard fan of this game now!"

"I don't get it. You've already spent over 60,000, why still use cheats? Can't you just hire someone to power-level for you?"

However, even more posts were cursing and crying foul at the same time.

They adamantly denied using cheats, crazily spamming posts and accusing *Power and Hegemony* of banning accounts indiscriminately. Uninformed netizens really thought they were being wronged.

Faced with this situation, Tao Chenggang instructed: "Hire a water army to post on the 17173 forum and Tieba for *Yulgang*, promoting how *Power and Hegemony* is banning cheating accounts. Also, have the water army promote it inside the *Yulgang* game, saying we've banned all the studios and paying players who use cheats!"

*Yulgang* was the big brother of free-to-play games. Although it was overrun with studios and cheaters, many players were still reluctant to leave.

Tao Chenggang's promotional strategy was very effective.

Over the next half a month, every day there were *Yulgang* players who switched over to *Power and Hegemony* because of its strict crackdown on cheats. Moreover, most of them used cheats themselves but couldn't stand that kind of environment either. Because you couldn't play without cheats, but using them made the game boring.

Now that there was *Power and Hegemony*, which was also free-to-play, *Yulgang* players who hadn't spent much money quit and switched camps without hesitation.

This phenomenon could easily start a trend.

There were even cases of entire guilds, with the leader bringing all his underlings, moving to *Power and Hegemony* together!

*Yulgang* lost a large number of players.

Beijing, 17game company.

CEO Dai Hong had previously operated *Thousand Years* and *Redmoon*.

He was holding the phone at this moment, his tone a little agitated: "Director Liu, we've been negotiating for over three months, how can your side just pull out like that?"

"Director Dai should know better than I do." The voice on the other end of the line was deep.

Dai Hong played dumb: "What is it?"

Director Liu on the phone said: "*Zhengtu*'s publicity was massive a few months ago, but luckily the game's completion level wasn't high, and now they've gone quiet to work on it again. But *Power and Hegemony* is gaining powerful momentum. Recently, it seems like a lot of posts from *Yulgang* players have appeared on their forum, all agreeing to move to *Power and Hegemony*."

"Those are just isolated cases!" Dai Hong argued.

*Yulgang*'s operator, 17game, was currently in acquisition talks with China.com.

Well, it was more like being acquired.

Shanda was also initially invested in by China.com. Because they weren't optimistic about Chen Tianqiao making games and couldn't reach an agreement, they simply let Chen Tianqiao go his own way.

Thus, China.com missed out on *The Legend of Mir*.

Now that China.com saw how hot the online gaming market was, it wanted to get in on the action again and acquire 17game.

That Director Liu was a senior executive at China.com, in charge of the acquisition negotiations.

Director Liu said: "The negotiations are temporarily suspended. After the Spring Festival, I will send a professional team to your company to carefully verify the operational status of *Yulgang*. Understand?"

China.com had plenty of money. They didn't have to acquire 17game; they had countless other options.

"Understood." Dai Hong hung up the phone.

He was very depressed.

Why was he always so unlucky?

When he was running *Thousand Years* and *Redmoon*, he ran into that monster, *The Legend of Mir*. Now with *Yulgang*, he ran into *Power and Hegemony*, and next, *Zhengtu* would be re-entering the scene.

It was too hard!

Dai Hong called over Sun Jingqing, who was in charge of operations: "How many players have we lost recently?"

Sun Jingqing said: "We've probably lost ten to twenty thousand active players. And it's not stopping; we're still losing them."

"We have to think of something," Dai Hong said.

Sun Jingqing, also a company shareholder, said gloomily: "What can I do? You want me to maintain the online user count and crack down on cheats, but the Korean developers won't cooperate. I don't have three heads and six arms; I can't satisfy so many demands."

Dai Hong said: "China.com has suspended negotiations. They're sending people to verify the game's operational status after the Spring Festival."

Sun Jingqing became even more depressed: "I told you a long time ago we needed to crack down on cheats and directly ban those who use them, but you were the one who stopped me, saying to keep negotiating with the Korean developers on the technical side. How do we crack down now? How many players in *Yulgang* don't use cheats? Are we going to ban all of them?"

"Ban the ones with malicious cheats, and turn a blind eye to the common ones," Dai Hong said.

Sun Jingqing retorted: "How do you judge what's malicious and what's common? A large-scale ban now is equivalent to forcing all our players to go to *Power and Hegemony*!"

Dai Hong fell silent.

This game could no longer be operated normally.

If they couldn't get the investment from China.com, the company could still muddle through, but what Dai Hong was thinking about was cashing out and leaving!

On the eve of the Spring Festival, during an event.

*Power and Hegemony* announced that its peak concurrent user count had surpassed 300,000!

As a shareholder of Bailian Technology, ByteDance's valuation was set to continue rising.

I forgot to schedule this chapter for publication. I only realized when I woke up from my nap at noon. My apologies.
